prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks (B007), Katori and Ye. The deciding facts are unchanged but sharper after reading the others. The magic-wavelength idea is a distinct invention: it removes the light shift while keeping many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which is what separates it from the comb prize of 2005 and from the ion-control prize of 2012, where single trapped ions were the subject. The 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and intercompared by independent laboratories with several species, so the result does not rest on one group's word. Kroll and Lindroth correctly stress that Ye's contribution goes beyond the first demonstration (record accuracy and stability, many-body clock physics), which supports two names without a third. I record that my position is not strengthened by the six-member count: several colleagues moved to B007 after the openings, and I treat the count as evidence of nothing beyond shared reasons. I weigh it only because those reasons, taken one by one, hold up when I test them against what I know of how instruments are validated. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1; what changed is that I now see the choice between B007 and B005 as a real trade between attribution and maturity on one side and scale on the other, and I am deciding it on those grounds.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap with the 2005 and 2012 lineage, together with the fact that the payoff most often cited, a redefinition of the second, has not yet happened and parts of the fundamental-physics reach (drifting constants, dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy) are still prospective. Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde, Lisdat and the PTB, SYRTE and NIST groups have real claims that a two-name citation cannot capture, and I cannot dismiss that. I think the concern is bounded: every prize omits someone, the three-name limit forces choices, and Katori carries both the proposal and the first strontium lattice clock, so the pair is defensible. If the committee decides that B005's breadth outweighs these points, B007 is the natural runner-up and B005 would not be a wrongful choice.

responses.point: Moved from B001 to B005 first, arguing that eight years of replication across many laboratories and a robust phenomenology suffice, and that the Yuan Cao omission is a consequence of the three-name limit rather than a disqualification.
responses.response: I accept the replication argument; it is the strongest part of the B005 case and I do not claim the field is fragile. Where I still differ is on what the committee can defend in public. A citation limited to the phenomena, as you propose, avoids the mechanism problem, but it cannot avoid the fact that the person who made the central 2018 measurements is not among the supplied names, and I do not accept that the three-name limit makes that a neutral fact. It is a consequence we would be choosing. For B007 the same limit leaves a smaller gap. I would not oppose your configuration if the committee prefers it, but my judgement is that it is better placed in a few years.

responses.point: Argues that maturity should be tested by the robustness of the flat-band and correlated-insulator phenomenology, not by whether the pairing mechanism is settled, and cites 1987 high-temperature superconductivity as precedent; also flags his own field proximity to moire theory.
responses.response: The 1987 precedent is fair, and I concede that an unsettled mechanism has not barred a prize before. I also respect that you flag your proximity to moire theory, which I would mirror with my own notes on field proximity. The difference I weigh is that in 1987 the discovery had a compact credit chain, whereas here the chain runs through at least six claimants, which you list yourself. Dropping Bistritzer, as Olsson and Mehlig would, makes the prediction half of the citation worse, and keeping him still leaves Cao out. On the science we are close, since you rank B007 second for clarity, so we differ mainly on how much attribution cleanliness should count.

responses.point: Prefers a two-name B007 citation worded around neutral-atom magic-wavelength trapping, opposes adding a third name, and flags adjacency to atom interferometry (B043) and his doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree on the two names and on wording the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realization at the 10^-18 level, and I have kept that language. Your Boulder connection is a documented link to the comb background, not to Katori or Ye, and I think the disclosure is sufficient. On B043 I remain unwilling to make it a second part: Chu already holds the prize, priority is spread over several 1991 experiments, and pairing it with B007 would blur precisely the attribution cleanliness that favours B007.

responses.point: Prefers B007 but lists Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat as uncredited and notes the repeated recognition of precision metrology (1997, 2005, 2012).
responses.response: I take the uncredited groups seriously and have said so in my own case against. My view is that the first strontium lattice clock and the magic-wavelength proposal are both Katori's, and that Ye's group carried the accuracy frontier, so the two names map onto the two parts of the achievement. The Takamoto and Ludlow contributions were made inside those programmes. On repeated recognition of metrology, I think the test is whether the invention is distinct, not whether the field has been honoured. Your own AMO background is a possible bias in favour, as you disclose, and I weigh your argument with that in mind; your point about multiple species and groups is the evidence I find most persuasive.

responses.point: Moved from B005 to B007, accepting that a prize omitting Bistritzer or Cao leaves a hole, and lists B012 as her second alternative.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning on the credit hole, and I note that you changed position for stated reasons rather than for numbers. On B012 as an alternative, which we share, I would keep it as an alternative rather than a second part: the diffuse flux is robust, but the source associations are only at the 3-4 sigma level and the credit within the IceCube collaboration is hard to defend with three names, which Mehlig raises fairly. I would not give B012 a part this year.

uncertainties: How much weight to give the pending redefinition of the second; the physics is mature, but the committee could reasonably wait for an unambiguous fundamental-physics result.
Whether lattice clocks are distinct enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems; I think so, but the question is a judgement, not a fact.
Whether the omission of Takamoto, Ludlow, Lemonde and Lisdat would be seen as a defect in the two-name citation.
For B005, whether the omission of Yuan Cao and the unresolved pairing mechanism will matter less in a few years, and so whether the committee is better placed to award it later rather than now.
My own experimental background makes me more inclined to weight demonstrated reproducibility of a measurement standard than conceptual breadth, which may bias me against B005, B001 and B025.
statement.conflict_note: My documented connections are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur and KTH's astroparticle group. B012 (IceCube) is in my own field of astroparticle physics, which is a field proximity and a possible perception issue; no tie to Halzen, Karle or Yoshida is recorded, and I do not propose B012 as a prize part, only as an alternative. No specific conflict is apparent for B007 or B005. As chair I have tried to summarize all positions fairly and my own preferred configuration is stated openly.
